item.title: Do Perturbation Predictors Learn Gene Interactions? Diagnosing Extrapolation in Agentic Screening
item.description: arXiv:2610.18880v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: High-throughput perturbation screens increasingly use machine-learning models to predict the effects of gene combinations that were never measured. A difficult case arises when both genes in a test pair were seen individually during training, but their combination was not. In this setting, standard OOD methods often fail because neither gene appears unfamiliar on its own. We therefore compare each model prediction with a simple additive prediction obtained by summing the two observed single-gene effects. The difference between them, which we call additive disagreement (AD), measures how much extra interaction effect the model introduces for an unseen combination. Across eight prediction methods and three Perturb-seq datasets, specialised neural predictors do not consistently outperform this simple additive baseline. More importantly, predictions with larger deviations from the additive baseline tend to have larger errors. Conventional output-based and embedding-based confidence signals are inconsistent across datasets and models, whereas AD remains informative across all evaluated compositional settings. We further study how this signal can guide decisions in an agentic perturbation-screening workflow. The code is available at https://github.com/zygao930/OOD.
item.dc:creator: Ziyuan Gao

item.title: Deep learning-based virtual perturbation reveals increasing heterogeneity of gene regulatory responses with aging
item.description: arXiv:2610.19029v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A central hypothesis in aging biology proposes that the gradual accumulation of stochastic molecular damage drives transcriptional deregulation (TD), ultimately leading to functional decline. However, existing single-cell analyses largely rely on static expression measurements and provide limited resolution of how regulatory responses change at the level of individual cells. Here, we leverage DKO, a deep learning framework that predicts cell-specific virtual gene perturbation effects from unperturbed transcriptomes, capturing cell-to-cell differences in regulatory context without requiring a reconstructed gene regulatory network or matched perturbation data. Applying DKO to single-cell transcriptomic datasets from humans, mice, Drosophila, and C. elegans revealed that the transcriptional consequences of perturbing the same gene became increasingly heterogeneous across cells with age, indicating that gene regulatory responses become less consistent and more dependent on cellular context. Furthermore, we find that cells with higher somatic mutation burdens have greater knockout-response variability, linking accumulated molecular damage to regulatory inconsistency. Within the same cellular populations, higher impact variability was also associated with higher senescence scores, linking transcriptional dysregulation to senescence-associated states. Our findings identify a progressive loss of regulatory robustness at both the gene and cell levels as a conserved feature of aging, linking stochastic molecular damage to increasing heterogeneity in cellular regulatory responses.
item.dc:creator: Yongjian He, Julia Hanna Haddad Guez, Xu-Wen Wang, Orr Levy
